title: Weaving together Indigenous Knowledge Systems, traditional fish harvesters’ rights, and inclusive marine carbon dioxide removal approaches
content:
Abstract
The climate crisis is leading to increased urgency to research carbon dioxide removal (CDR) techniques, including marine CDR (mCDR), which aim to enhance CO2 storage within the ocean. Research is currently on-going to develop viable mCDR techniques that can remove carbon efficiently, safely, and at scale. Nation states are tasked with regulation of mCDR activities, and international bodies affirm the fundamental rights of Indigenous People with principles of self-governance and management of natural resources. To leverage available resources, it is advisable that Indigenous People’s rights to inclusive engagement, partnership, and co-design are recognized given their generational connections with nature, the oceans, and long-standing management of their own natural resources. There are immense benefits for mCDR projects to develop opportunities for co-leadership, co-development, co-production, and co-ownership with Indigenous People, especially for traditional fish harvesters and aquaculture farmers. Additionally, Indigenous People can benefit from involvement with mCDR projects through capacity development, enhanced resources, and opportunities for partnership and/or co-ownership. As presented from our Indigenous authors point of view, this perspective shares examples of Indigenous Knowledge Systems from various Indigenous view points and how they relate to mCDR. This includes those of the Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick, Canada and the Makah Tribe in the U.S. Pacific Northwest, along with lessons from the Mi’kmaq Nation in Canada. We present reasons for the mCDR sector to prioritize engagement with Indigenous communities and provide recommendations for engagement. This perspective aims to offer insights that can help inform frameworks and guidance that can be developed for individual projects and diverse audiences; actors who may be interested in these perspectives and future frameworks include mCDR practitioners interested in engaging Indigenous communities, decision-makers developing policies and guidance for mCDR projects, and Indigenous members who may be interested in being involved with mCDR.
